Record check 2026-09-20 (user has a TypeSafe plan as of today; "parked" no longer applies). Corrections and gaps against the 09-19 audit:

1. Context is 64k total, 32k for state + the longest question (not a flat 32k). Rate limits 250k tokens/s and 1,200 req/min, dynamic; higher on enterprise via sales@typesafe.ai. Current model jev-1.13.0; aliases jev-latest and jev-preview both point at it; GET /v1/models lists what an account may use. Pin the exact version in anything we record, never the alias (same rule as the driver's context_window: state it, never infer).
2. Privacy: "We will not train or fine tune any AI/ML models on your prompts or other Input"; Input is not disclosed except to service providers; retention period unspecified; no zero-data-retention option. So the invariant's privacy clause is softened (no training) but not resolved (content leaves the machine and sits for an unstated time). redact.ts exists and should run before any send.
3. JS SDK is @typesafe-ai/sdk and needs Node ≥20; sofar requires Node ≥18 and CLAUDE.md forbids new deps without a Decision. Use fetch against POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY) — zero deps, Node 18 has fetch.
4. Alternative route: Cloudflare Workers AI lists typesafe/jev with no gate (POST /accounts/{id}/ai/run, model typesafe/jev). Not needed now that a direct plan exists.
5. Confidence is a statistic of the distribution: for 3 options (3·pmax−1)/2, i.e. (n·pmax−1)/(n−1); Noul carries none, use |p−0.5|. Docs: no structural invariants across questions (P(A)+P(not A) across two Nouls need not be 1); never carry a threshold from one question type to another; validate thresholds on our own data.
6. jev-1.13 known limitations page: literal reading (scoping words and negations at face value), no counting, weak on numeric representations, dates read as text, indirection and double negatives degrade, large irrelevant state distracts, adversarial state moves the answer, contradictory instructions vs criteria confuse it, no text generation. Consequences for sofar: staleness, counts and timestamps stay in code; state is selected lexically first (the existing index) and only the candidates are sent; agent-written record text is untrusted input, so every judge output is advisory (warning in a tool result), never a mutation, never a block (BD22 best-effort).
7. Self-consistency cookbook: per-question probability std dev 0.0102 across 15 repeats, far below LLMs. Near-deterministic, not byte-deterministic; fold and graph keep their pure contracts and judge outputs live outside them.
8. Structured criteria (what / not_for / examples per option; summary / signals per level) and instructions that cite state paths in backticks are directly usable to encode our decision guards and rejected approaches as criteria.
9. TypeSafe ships a Claude Code plugin (claude plugin install typesafe@typesafe-ai) so the agent itself can call Jev in a session; that is the operator's process and not sofar's concern, but it means a sofar session may already have the skill loaded.
10. Still absent anywhere: architecture paper, public calibration curve, third-party replication. Thresholds must come from our own ground truth (bench-refresh hidden tests, and the record's own history: decisions later superseded, approaches later re-proposed).

The 09-19 waitlist answer note and the roadmap-h2 audit note stand; nothing in them is wrong.

Feature catalogue (2026-09-20): what a cheap calibrated judge unlocks in sofar, grouped by where it can run. Constraint first: 70–500 ms means never on a hook, statusline or shim (speed T2, 100 ms). It fits three places: WRITE time (inside an MCP tool call or the driver between sessions), PULL time (find, related, why, review), and OFFLINE (index pass, tune, bench loss study). Anything a hook must show is judged at write time and stored in the derived index or as an enrichment event with a producer field (the roadmap-h2 design), then read cheaply. Cost is not a factor: ten questions over a full 16k digest is about $0.0007; a heavy day of write-backs is cents.

A. WRITE-TIME GUARDS (highest leverage: the write-back is the event the next session reads first)
A1 Write-back quality gate in sofar_end_session: Score next_action on levels {vague, names a task, names a task and a concrete first step, executable verbatim}; low score returns a warning asking for a better one. Noul "does the summary describe a decision that was not logged?" and "an operational fact worth repo memory?" (the decision / fact / note distinction agents get wrong; repo-memory-capture already wants this).
A2 Re-proposal guard in sofar_log_decision: Noul per rejected approach (criteria built from the rejection text) "does this decision re-propose R?"; warning with the rejected item cited. Directly targets bench claim C3.
A3 Contradiction guard: Noul per standing constraint "does this decision contradict D-n?", same-initiative and cross-initiative (candidates chosen by the existing index, then judged; state stays under 32k). Extends drift-hardening decision guards and cross-initiative-conflicts.
A4 Decision hygiene: Noul "does `because` give a reason or restate the choice?"; Choice {decision, operational fact, note} to route a misfiled write with a hint.
A5 Task-done evidence: on sofar_update_task(done), Noul "does the note cite evidence (test run, commit, criteria)?"; warning only. Acceptance-criteria law made checkable.

B. DRIVER (unattended runs; between sessions, latency irrelevant)
B1 Progress judge: today stall = no status change. Noul over {task text, write-back, diff stat, test output} "did this session advance the task?" plus Score "how done against the acceptance text?"; a task_done handoff needs status AND judged completion. Targets C4 wasted sessions and C5 rework.
B2 Richer handoff reason: Choice {task_done, partial, stalled, blocked_on_user, worked_wrong_task, scope_creep}; needs_user today fires only on status=blocked, but the write-back prose often names an operator decision.
B3 Pre-flight: before launching, Noul "is this task specified well enough to act without asking?"; low → mark needs_user and skip the launch instead of burning a session.
B4 Route hints: Score task complexity on described levels → effort; Choice model; fills only what the run left open (routing.ts rule: run over task).
B5 Next-task sanity: Noul "after this write-back, is the plan's next task still the right one?"; low → nudge the operator, never reorder the plan.

C. INJECTION AND CONTEXT (judged at write time, read by hooks)
C1 Relevance-scored digest: at end_session the next task is known, so Score every decision, note, rejected approach and repo-memory line for relevance to it; store scores in the index; the SessionStart hook injects top-k and truncates the least relevant instead of the last. Small token win (~1% of a session) but a real orientation win (digest-signal goal).
C2 Adjacency to aboutness: "…and 34 more adjacent records" becomes the three that actually bear on the next task (Noul per adjacent initiative).
C3 Constraint classification: at scale, Choice per decision {standing constraint, history, superseded} so "obey verbatim (6)" stays six and not sixty.

D. PULL SURFACES
D1 Semantic re-ranking for find / related / why: candidates from the lexical index, ranked by Score; the citation grammar stays closed and lexical (contract).
D2 Why-questions answered by citation: "why no pid files?" → lexical candidates → Choice over candidate decisions "which answers this?" with confidence → the answer is an id, no text generation needed. Targets C8.

E. OFFLINE
E1 Bench-refresh: a "sofar + judge" arm; Jev as a calibrated blind reviewer for C5; loss-row classification into the D5/D10 taxonomy at near-zero cost.
E2 Tune/suggest: cause labelling is excluded by design; offer at most an opt-in labelled view, never change the detectors.
E3 Calibration study on our own record: judge all ~280 decisions for constraint-vs-history and every rejected approach against later decisions; the record already knows which were superseded or re-proposed, so it is free ground truth for thresholds. This is the right FIRST step: measure before wiring anything.

Architecture for all of it: one Judge seam (noul / choice / score over a state object) with a deterministic default provider (today's counts and lexical rules answering with confidence 1.0 or 0.5) and an opt-in Jev provider via fetch; enrichment events carry producer and model version; redaction before send; outputs advisory only. Needs the opt-in Decision naming SPEC Architectural invariants and felt-cost D3 before the provider exists; the seam, the question set and E3 as a scratch script need no ruling.

Suggested order when work opens: E3 (measure) → A1/A2 (write-time guards) → B1/B3 (driver) → C1 (digest) → D2 → E1.

payload.text:
LAYA / LAYA-MLX vs JEV (2026-09-21, user asked about github.com/mizorewww/laya-mlx, which is marketed as "50x faster than Jev").

WHAT IT IS. Laya (Convai Innovations, github NandhaKishorM/laya, Apache-2.0 weights on HF) is an open-weight copy of Jev's shape: the same primitives choice/score/noul (even the name "noul"), "RLCD" training, "System 1" framing. It is a ModernBERT-large (421M, 512 ctx) or mmBERT-base (322M, 1024 ctx) encoder with decision heads. Three checkpoints: laya (English), laya-multilingual, laya-typed-decisions (fine-tuned). laya-mlx is an unofficial third-party port of that model to Apple MLX (Python ≥3.11, macOS 14+, Apple Silicon only). It is a runtime, not a new model: it matched upstream's answers on 63/63 questions in FP32 and FP16.

THE 50x CLAIM. Neither README says 50x. Upstream claims 6–7.8x (T4, 32.8 ms vs Jev's third-party p50 of 236–276 ms). laya-mlx measures 7.39 ms p50 (multilingual FP16, M3 Max 40-core, warm, 91-token input, load excluded). Against third-party Jev numbers that is ~32–37x. Against our own 1.1 Jev p50 of 402 ms it is ~54x. But our 402 ms is a network round trip carrying ~7.7k tokens of state and ~14 questions per request (325,265 tokens / 42 requests). Like for like, Laya cannot take that request at all: its limit is 512/1024 tokens INCLUDING instructions and options. Each question also re-encodes state+question as its own row, so cost grows linearly with question count × state length (the laya-mlx README says it does not reuse state hidden states). laya-typed-decisions takes 1,000 ms for 10 questions at full 1024 ctx on M3 Max, which is slower than our Jev batch. The 50x holds only for tiny inputs and a warm resident model.

ACCURACY (upstream's own report; Jev figures are third-party and were never measured by them). typed-decisions 0.766 vs Jev 0.727, but that is the fine-tuned checkpoint on that benchmark's own training split. The base checkpoints score 0.362/0.342 there, BELOW the 0.461 majority-class baseline (their BENCHMARKS.md says "near chance on typed-decisions zero-shot"). Laya takes one state per call, so each sample is its own call, and B puts the task before the decision so a right-truncation cannot drop it. Question wording and criteria are Jev's.

Jev 0.715 / 0.698 · typed-decisions 0.672 / 0.664 · English 0.608 / 0.589 · multilingual 0.382 / 0.554. Multilingual collapses to one_off: it predicts a constraint 1.6% of the time. Jev 0.678 / 0.787 / 0.211 / 0.141 · English 0.691 / 0.753 / 0.206 / 0.086 · typed-decisions 0.548 / 0.701 / 0.240 / 0.143 · multilingual 0.552 / 0.572 / 0.303 / 0.211.
